title: Dimension lower bound for each rational closed-fibre component of a finite type algebra map
statement: Let $k$ be a field, let $B$ and $C$ be commutative finite type $k$-algebras [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra], and suppose that $C$ is an integral domain. Let $\varphi:B\to C$ be a unital $k$-algebra homomorphism and put $P=\ker\varphi$. Let $\mathfrak m$ be a maximal ideal of $B$ such that the structure map $k\to B/\mathfrak m$ is an isomorphism. Set $J=(\varphi(b):b\in\mathfrak m)\subseteq C$, the ideal generated by the indicated elements. Then every irreducible component $W$ [def-weil-irreducible-components] of $\operatorname{Spec}(C/J)$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] satisfies $$\dim W\geq\dim C-\dim(B/P).$$ Here $\dim W$ is topological Krull dimension with the subspace topology [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension], and the dimensions of rings are Krull dimensions [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. The ring dimensions on the right are finite nonnegative integers. If $C/J$ is the zero ring, the assertion about components is vacuous.

source.place: Tag 0B2L, lemma-dimension-fibres-locally-algebraic, (2)(a); affine k-rational closed-fibre component formulation

proof.text: Put $A=B/P$, $H=C/J$ and $L=\operatorname{Frac}(C)$. The kernel $P$ is prime because $C$ is a nonzero domain: $bb'\in P$ implies $\varphi(b)\varphi(b')=0$, so $b\in P$ or $b'\in P$, and $1\notin P$. Thus $A\hookrightarrow C$ is an inclusion of domains; put $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$, embedded in $L$ by $\bar b/\bar s\mapsto\varphi(b)/\varphi(s)$. Finite algebra generators of $B$ over $k$ descend to generators of $A$; finite algebra generators of $C$ over $k$ also generate $C$ over $B$ and over $A$, since the structure maps are compatible with $\varphi$. Their images generate $H$ over $k$. These are direct applications of the finite-generation definition.

source.place: Tag 0B2L, proof of (2), affine setup; finite-generation definition Tag 00F3.

proof.text: Apply the finite-type-domain dimension theorem to $C$ and $A$. It gives finite nonnegative integers $\dim C=\operatorname{trdeg}_k L$ and $\dim A=\operatorname{trdeg}_k K$. For the field tower $k\subseteq K\subseteq L$, the tower identity gives $\operatorname{trdeg}_k L=\operatorname{trdeg}_k K+\operatorname{trdeg}_K L$. Since the left side is finite, all these cardinal degrees are finite integers. Hence $d:=\dim C-\dim A=\operatorname{trdeg}_K L\geq0$.

source.place: Tag 0B2L, proof of (2), displayed generic transcendence-degree calculation; Tag 00P0 and Fields Tag 030H.

proof.text: The residue field $\kappa(P)$ of $B$ identifies with $K$: the fraction $b/s$ modulo $PB_P$ maps to $\bar b/\bar s$, and the inverse takes this latter fraction to the class of $b/s$; $s\notin P$ is precisely the condition $\bar s\ne0$. The generic-fibre localization theorem, applied to $A\hookrightarrow C$, identifies $F=K\otimes_A C$ with $S^{-1}C$, where $S$ is the image of $A\setminus\{0\}$. Its hypotheses hold because the inclusion is injective, and $F$ is a nonzero domain. This is also the $B$-fibre $C\otimes_B\kappa(P)$: the maps $c\otimes u\mapsto u\otimes c$ and $u\otimes c\mapsto c\otimes u$ are inverse, using the quotient action of $B$ through $A$. As a $K$-algebra $F$ is generated by $1\otimes c_i$, for any finite $A$-algebra generators $c_i$ of $C$: substitute these generators in a polynomial expression for each tensor factor and sum the finitely many pure tensors.

source.place: Tag 0B2L, proof of (2), generic fibre at the image of the generic point; algebraic localization description Tag 00DK and residue-field definition Tag 00CO.

proof.text: The injection $F=S^{-1}C\hookrightarrow L$ sends $c/s$ to the same fraction. Its fraction field is $L$: it contains $C$, so each $a/b\in L$ is the quotient of the images of $a,b\in C$, and conversely all its fractions lie in $L$. Localizing the domain $F$ at its zero prime inverts every nonzero element, so $F_{(0)}=\operatorname{Frac}(F)=L$ and its residue field is $L$. A field has just the prime ideal $(0)$, so its ring dimension is zero by the chain definition. Apply the dimension-at-a-point formula to the finite type $K$-algebra $F$ at $(0)$: $$\dim_{(0)}\operatorname{Spec}F=\dim F_{(0)}+\operatorname{trdeg}_K L=0+d=d.$$ The zero prime of $F$ contracts to the zero prime of $C$, which contracts to $P$ in $B$. Thus the local fibre dimension denoted $\dim_{(0)}(C/B)$ in the bounded-open theorem is exactly $d$.

source.place: Tag 0B2L, proof of (2), equality with the dimension at the generic point of the generic fibre; algebra Tag 00P1.

proof.text: If $H=0$, its spectrum has no irreducible components and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise fix a component $W$ of $\operatorname{Spec}H$. Since $B/\mathfrak m=k$ through the given structure isomorphism, $\kappa(\mathfrak m)=k$: localization of the field $B/\mathfrak m$ changes nothing. The closed-fibre algebra $E=C\otimes_B k$ is isomorphic to $H$. Explicitly $c\otimes a\mapsto a\bar c$ and $\bar c\mapsto c\otimes1$ are inverse; the latter is well defined because each $\varphi(b)$ for $b\in\mathfrak m$ acts by zero in the tensor product, and $c\otimes a=ac\otimes1$ by balancing. Thus this is the actual fibre over $\mathfrak m$, with its specified $k$-structure.

source.place: Tag 0B2L (1) and (2)(a), rational closed-fibre identification; fibre-ring definition in Tag 07BZ.

proof.text: By the spectrum-component theorem write $W=V_H(\bar{\mathfrak q})$ for a minimal prime $\bar{\mathfrak q}$ of $H$. Its inverse image $\mathfrak q$ under $C\twoheadrightarrow H$ is prime. The ideal $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$ contains $\mathfrak m$ and is proper, hence equals $\mathfrak m$ by maximality. A component $V_H(\bar{\mathfrak r})$ containing $\bar{\mathfrak q}$ satisfies $\bar{\mathfrak r}\subseteq\bar{\mathfrak q}$, so minimality forces equality. The dimension-at-a-point/components theorem for the finite type $k$-algebra $H$ therefore gives $n:=\dim_{\bar{\mathfrak q}}\operatorname{Spec}H=\dim W$, a finite nonnegative integer. The isomorphism $E\simeq H$ from Step 5 induces inverse maps of spectra by functoriality, hence a homeomorphism. It carries the point of the fibre above $\mathfrak q$ to $\bar{\mathfrak q}$, since the map to $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ has that kernel. Matching open neighbourhoods under this homeomorphism and using invariance of their dimensions identifies their minima. Thus $\dim_{\mathfrak q}(C/B)=n$.

source.place: Tag 0B2L (2)(a), passage from local fibre dimension to each component; algebra Tags 00ES and 00OT; topology Tag 0055.

proof.text: Apply the bounded-open fibre-dimension theorem to the finite type map $B\to C$ at $\mathfrak q$ with the integer $n$ of Step 6. It supplies an open neighbourhood $V$ of $\mathfrak q$ in $\operatorname{Spec}C$ on which every local fibre dimension is at most $n$. Since $C$ is a domain, $(0)$ is prime and its closure is $V_C(0)=\operatorname{Spec}C$ by the prime-closure theorem. Therefore every nonempty open, in particular $V$, contains $(0)$: otherwise its closed complement would contain $(0)$ and hence its entire closure. Applying the bound at $(0)$ and Step 4 yields $$\dim C-\dim(B/P)=d=\dim_{(0)}(C/B)\leq n=\dim W.$$ This proves the assertion for each $W$ and completes the proof.

The item is a correct affine special case of Stacks 0B2L(2)(a) (varieties.tex l.3953): a component W of the rational closed fibre has dim W = dim_x of the fibre at W's generic point, because minimality leaves only W through that point. The seven steps follow the source proof and each cited node's statement says what the step uses. Steps 1-2: P is prime, and the 00P0 node plus the 030H tower give d = trdeg_K L >= 0. Step 3: kappa(P) = Frac(B/P); the generic-fibre localization node gives F = S^{-1}C, a domain of finite type over K. Step 4: the 00P1 node at (0) gives dim_(0) Spec F = d, and Q' = 0 because F embeds in L. Step 5: C tensor_B k = C/J. Step 6: the 00ES nodes and the 00OT node give dim_{q-bar} Spec H = dim W, carried to the fibre point by the homeomorphism. Step 7: the 00QH node gives an open V containing q, and (0) lies in V by irreducibility, so d <= dim W. Small cases checked: xy over k[t]; a non-dominant k[s,t] -> k[x] (both a nonempty fibre and an empty one, where the claim is vacuous); B = k. The dependency closure has no cycle.
